body.passage_title: How Children Learn to Read

body.passage:
When people think of urban pollution, they usually picture smog-filled skies or plastic-choked rivers. Rarely do they consider the constant, invisible assault on their ears. Yet noise pollution has become one of the most widespread environmental problems of modern city life, affecting hundreds of millions of people worldwide. According to the World Health Organization, traffic noise alone is now the second most harmful environmental stressor in Western Europe, after air pollution.

The sources of urban noise are numerous and persistent. Road traffic remains the dominant contributor, with lorries, motorcycles and honking horns producing sound levels that frequently exceed 70 decibels on major streets — a level considered harmful over prolonged exposure. Airports impose additional burdens on nearby neighbourhoods, while construction sites, nightclubs and even leaf blowers add to the daily din. Unlike chemical pollutants, noise leaves no physical residue, which is precisely why it has historically been neglected by regulators and the public alike.

The consequences, however, are far from harmless. Chronic exposure to noise triggers the body's stress response, raising blood pressure and releasing hormones such as cortisol. Research has linked long-term noise exposure to increased risks of heart disease, sleep disturbance and cognitive impairment in children. A landmark German study found that children living near busy airports performed worse in reading tests than their quieter counterparts. Sleep, in particular, suffers: even noises that do not wake a sleeper can fragment sleep cycles, leaving people exhausted despite a full night in bed.

Certain groups are disproportionately affected. Low-income households often cannot afford to move away from motorways or industrial zones, and their homes may lack double glazing or sound insulation. This means the burden of noise falls most heavily on those with the fewest resources to escape it, turning noise into a matter of social equity as much as public health.

Fortunately, cities are beginning to respond. Paris has installed noise-detecting cameras that fine excessively loud vehicles, while Barcelona is redesigning its streets to reduce traffic volume through 'superblocks' that prioritise pedestrians. Simple measures — planting trees, resurfacing roads with quieter materials, enforcing night-time flight restrictions — can cut noise levels significantly at relatively low cost. Some planners now argue that noise maps should be treated as seriously as air quality maps when deciding where to build schools, hospitals and housing.

Ultimately, tackling noise pollution requires a shift in mindset. Because we cannot see it, we have learned to tolerate it. But a city that protects its citizens' hearing, as well as their lungs, is not an impossible dream — it is simply a matter of political will and careful design.

When the technology company Novatek announced the AquaSense smartwatch in January, expectations were high. The device, which promised to track swimmers' heart rates underwater without a chest strap, was hailed by industry analysts as a potential game-changer. The company scheduled the launch for June, and pre-orders opened within days of the announcement.

By April, however, cracks were beginning to appear. During routine testing, engineers discovered that the waterproof seal degraded faster than expected when exposed to chlorinated pool water. Although the watch remained functional, the sensor readings became unreliable after roughly two hundred hours of swimming. Releasing a product that failed to meet its own advertising claims would have exposed the company to lawsuits and lasting damage to its reputation.

The management team faced a difficult choice. Pushing ahead with the June launch would have satisfied impatient customers and investors, many of whom had already paid deposits. Postponing, on the other hand, meant losing the crucial summer sales season, when swimming-related products sell best. After a tense week of meetings, the chief executive, Dr. Lena Okafor, announced a delay until October, along with a full refund programme for early pre-order customers.

The decision was not universally popular. Several retail partners complained publicly that the delay left gaps in their summer catalogues, and Novatek's share price fell by twelve per cent in the week following the announcement. Some commentators even suggested that the company had exaggerated the original problem to buy time and fix unrelated software issues.

Internally, however, the extra months proved invaluable. The engineering team redesigned the seal using a new polymer compound, and the improved version passed independent laboratory tests with readings that remained accurate for over a thousand hours. The delay also allowed the software team to add a coaching feature that had originally been planned for a later model.

When the AquaSense finally launched in October, reviews were overwhelmingly positive. The device sold out within three weeks, and the company reported that nearly seventy per cent of customers who had requested refunds returned to buy the improved version. Dr. Okafor later reflected that the delay, though painful at the time, had probably saved the product. 'We could have shipped something that worked most of the time,' she told a business journal. 'Instead, we shipped something that worked all of the time, and customers noticed the difference.'

Every Saturday morning, the empty car park behind Riverside Town Hall is transformed into one of the region's most beloved attractions: the Riverside Farmers' Market. What began fifteen years ago with just six stalls selling vegetables and homemade jam has grown into a weekly event that draws over two thousand visitors and supports more than eighty local producers.

The market's success is largely credited to its strict 'local-first' policy. Every vendor must live or farm within fifty kilometres of the town, a rule introduced by the founding committee to guarantee that money spent at the market stays in the community. This policy has not been without controversy, however. A few years ago, a well-known baker from a neighbouring county applied for a stall and was refused, prompting heated debate in the local press. The committee eventually upheld its decision, arguing that the market's identity depended on its strictly local character.

Beyond fresh produce, the market has become a social hub. Regulars often spend as much time chatting with neighbours as they do shopping, and a volunteer-run café tent offers coffee and pastries while local musicians perform. According to a recent survey conducted by the town council, nearly seventy per cent of visitors said the sense of community was their main reason for attending, ranking it above price and even product quality.

The market has also had a measurable economic impact. A university study found that surrounding shops, particularly the hardware store and the bookshop, report significantly higher takings on market Saturdays than on other days of the week. Several empty shop units in the town centre have been rented out since the market became established, reversing a decade of decline.

Nevertheless, challenges remain. Rising stall fees, needed to cover the cost of insurance and cleaning, have pushed some smaller growers out, and organisers are now considering a sliding scale so that the smallest producers pay less. Weather is another constant concern; during last winter's storms, attendance dropped by almost half, forcing the committee to dip into its reserves. Despite these difficulties, the committee remains confident. As its chairperson, Margaret Okafor, put it: 'The market isn't really about vegetables. It's about people deciding what kind of town they want to live in.'

body.model_answer: Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to express my concern about an inaccurate forecast issued by your service last weekend. On Friday, the forecast for Saturday clearly stated that the whole region would enjoy sunny skies with only a slight chance of clouds. Based on this information, my family and I organised a picnic in the countryside with some relatives we had not seen for months. Unfortunately, by early afternoon the sky became completely overcast, and a violent thunderstorm broke out. We had no umbrellas or raincoats, so we were soaked and had to abandon our picnic. Worse still, one of my cousins slipped on the muddy path and injured her ankle. I understand that weather forecasting is a complex science and that predictions can never be perfect. However, I believe your service could improve in two ways. First, forecasts should be updated more frequently, especially when conditions change suddenly. Second, a mobile alert system warning people of unexpected weather would help the public adjust their plans in time. I hope you will take these suggestions into consideration. Yours faithfully, Minh Tran

body.model_answer: Dear Lan, Thank you so much for welcoming me to your village last week. I really enjoyed my stay, and I wanted to share some of my impressions before they fade. Before this trip, I had never seen rice farming up close, so the vast green fields stretching along the river amazed me. I followed your uncle to the paddy early one morning and watched him plant seedlings in neat rows, knee-deep in water. I was surprised by how much of the work is still done by hand, even though the delta floods regularly and the soil is so fertile. Honestly, I had expected more machines, like the tractors I have seen on television. What impressed me most was how carefully farmers read the weather and the tides; their knowledge comes from years of experience, not textbooks. However, I also noticed that incomes seem low, and many young people leave for the city. One idea might be for the village to form a cooperative that sells rice directly to city shops under a local brand name. That could raise prices and keep more profit in the community. Please thank your family again for their kindness, and let me know if you can visit me next month. Warm wishes, Minh

body.model_answer: Dear Mr Nguyen, I am writing regarding the letter I received on 3rd June, in which you announced that your company will move from weekly to fortnightly deliveries starting next month. While I understand that rising transport costs may have influenced this decision, I am concerned about the impact it will have on my business. As the owner of a small grocery store, I rely on fresh produce arriving every week. With deliveries only every two weeks, some items such as dairy products and fresh vegetables will spoil before they can be sold, which will lead to noticeable financial losses. Moreover, my customers expect a regular supply of fresh goods, and any shortage could encourage them to shop at larger supermarkets instead. I would therefore like to propose an alternative: perhaps we could keep the weekly schedule for perishable items while combining non-perishable goods into fortnightly deliveries. Alternatively, a small surcharge for weekly service might be acceptable to us. I would appreciate it if you could reconsider this change or contact me to discuss possible solutions. I look forward to your reply. Yours sincerely, Lan Pham

Dear Alex,

How are you doing? I hope everything is going well at university. I'm writing to tell you about a fascinating trip I took last weekend to the big suspension bridge here in the city, where a guide explained how engineers design such huge structures to withstand strong winds.

First of all, I learned that wind can be extremely dangerous for long bridges. When air flows around the deck, it can create vibrations that, if ignored, may grow until the whole structure twists or even collapses. The guide mentioned a famous disaster in 1940 when a bridge in the United States was destroyed by wind alone.

To prevent this, modern bridges use several clever features. The deck is built with open trusses so the wind can pass straight through instead of pushing against a solid wall. Engineers also add aerodynamic shapes, dampers and flexible cables that absorb movement and keep the bridge stable even in storms.

Honestly, it was one of the most interesting tours I have ever taken. Why don't you come and visit the bridge with me next month? We could walk across it and I'll point out the design details myself.

The article also explained that when people do not get enough sleep, their concentration suffers and they forget things more easily. This is why students who stay up late before an exam often perform worse than expected.

The most fascinating part was learning how bats find their way in the dark. I found it amazing that such small animals have such a sophisticated natural radar system. body.model_answer: Dear Tom, How are you doing? I hope everything is going well with your new job. I am writing to tell you about something fascinating I read recently: the invention of refrigeration. Before the nineteenth century, people preserved food with salt, ice or smoke, which was inconvenient and often unsafe. In 1834, an American inventor named Jacob Perkins built the first practical vapour-compression system, and later pioneers such as Carl von Linde made refrigeration reliable enough for homes and businesses. What struck me most was how deeply refrigerators have changed our habits. Nowadays, we can shop once a week instead of every day, keep fresh meat and dairy for days, and enjoy food imported from other continents. Families also cook less frequently and store leftovers safely, which reduces waste. Looking ahead, I believe manufacturers should focus on making refrigerators more energy-efficient and environmentally friendly, perhaps by using natural coolants and smart sensors that adjust the temperature automatically. This would cut electricity bills and protect the planet. What do you think about this? Write back soon and tell me your opinion. Best wishes, Minh

Write an essay of at least 250 words giving your opinion with reasons and examples.

_provenance.cefr_reasoning: The prompt requires an opinion essay of at least 250 words on an abstract topic (first impressions and character), demanding argumentation, cohesive devices, and a range of B2 vocabulary and grammar. body.model_answer:
In today's fast-paced world, we frequently form opinions about others within seconds of meeting them, whether in job interviews, social gatherings or everyday encounters. While some people trust these initial judgements as an accurate reflection of character, I largely believe that first impressions are unreliable, although they can occasionally offer useful clues.

On the one hand, there are reasons why first impressions sometimes carry genuine information. Psychologists argue that humans evolved to make rapid judgements as a survival mechanism, and in many cases these snap decisions are based on observable behaviour such as body language, eye contact and tone of voice. For instance, a candidate who arrives late and dressed carelessly for an interview may indeed reveal a lack of professionalism. In this sense, first impressions can act as an initial filter that is not entirely baseless.

On the other hand, research consistently shows that such judgements are frequently distorted by bias. We tend to favour people who are physically attractive, well-dressed or similar to ourselves, regardless of their actual abilities or personality. Moreover, a person may behave unnaturally when nervous, as many candidates do in interviews, leading observers to wrongly conclude that they are unfriendly or incompetent. A shy student, for example, might appear arrogant on a first meeting simply because he or she speaks little, whereas closer acquaintance would reveal a warm and thoughtful individual.

In conclusion, although first impressions may occasionally provide useful signals, they are too easily influenced by stereotypes and circumstance to be trusted as a measure of true character. In my view, we should treat them as a starting point rather than a conclusion, and allow time and further interaction to shape our final judgement of others.

body.model_answer:
The recent reopening of our city museum after a two-year renovation has sparked considerable debate among residents. While some people celebrate the investment in culture, others argue that public funds should have been directed towards hospitals or roads. In my view, although basic services are undeniably important, spending money on the museum was justified.

On the one hand, critics of the renovation have a reasonable point. Healthcare and transport directly affect people's daily lives, and a hospital with modern equipment can literally save lives. Similarly, poorly maintained roads cause accidents and waste commuters' time. From this perspective, renovating a building full of old objects may seem like a luxury that a city with limited budgets cannot afford.

On the other hand, a well-restored museum brings benefits that are less obvious but equally valuable. First, it attracts tourists, who spend money in local hotels, restaurants and shops, thereby creating jobs and increasing tax revenue. Second, museums serve an educational purpose: schoolchildren who visit exhibitions often develop a deeper understanding of history and science than textbooks alone can provide. Finally, a renovated museum becomes a shared public space where citizens of all ages can gather, which strengthens the community's sense of identity.

In my opinion, the two goals are not mutually exclusive. The renovation project was likely funded by a cultural budget that could not legally be spent on medical equipment, and the improved museum will generate income that can, in turn, support other services. Moreover, a city that invests only in practical infrastructure risks becoming a place with nothing worth visiting.

In conclusion, while hospitals and roads must remain priorities, the money spent on the museum was not wasted. A thriving cultural institution complements, rather than competes with, essential public services, and our newly reopened museum will benefit the city for decades to come.

Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write an essay of at least 250 words.

body.model_answer:
In recent years, an increasing number of adults have decided to learn a musical instrument, challenging the traditional belief that music education belongs to childhood. While some argue that only children can truly master an instrument, I believe that adults gain equally valuable, and in some ways more meaningful, benefits from learning music.

Those who favour starting young point to several convincing arguments. First of all, children's brains are highly adaptable, which allows them to absorb new skills, such as reading music and coordinating their fingers, more quickly and naturally than adults. In addition, children usually have fewer responsibilities and more free time, so they can practise consistently over many years. Many professional musicians, after all, began training before the age of ten.

However, I would argue that adult learners enjoy distinct advantages of their own. Unlike children, adults choose to learn an instrument out of genuine personal interest, and this intrinsic motivation often makes them more disciplined and persistent. Moreover, learning music as an adult offers well-documented benefits for mental health: it reduces stress, improves concentration, and provides a satisfying escape from the pressures of work. A friend of mine, for example, took up the guitar at thirty-five after a stressful period in her career, and she says that practising each evening has noticeably improved her mood and confidence.

Admittedly, adults may never reach the technical fluency of someone who started at five, but for the vast majority of learners, the goal is personal enjoyment rather than a professional career.

In conclusion, although early training has clear advantages for those aiming at mastery, I firmly believe that learning an instrument as an adult is deeply worthwhile. The combination of motivation, discipline and psychological benefits makes it a rewarding pursuit at any age.

body.model_answer:
In recent years, the expansion of successful local businesses has become a common phenomenon, and the plan by a well-known bakery to open a second shop is no exception. While this development offers several clear benefits, it also raises concerns that deserve careful consideration. In my view, the advantages outweigh the drawbacks, provided the bakery manages its growth responsibly.

To begin with, the most obvious benefit is job creation. A second shop would require bakers, sales assistants and delivery staff, which would reduce unemployment in the neighbourhood and give young people valuable work experience. In addition, residents of the new area would gain convenient access to fresh, high-quality products without travelling to the original location. This improved accessibility could even encourage healthier eating habits, as freshly baked bread is generally a better choice than packaged supermarket alternatives.

Nevertheless, there are legitimate concerns. Some customers fear that expanding production may force the bakery to compromise on quality, since maintaining the same handmade standards across two sites is challenging. Furthermore, if the new shop competes directly with smaller, family-run bakeries, it could drive them out of business, reducing variety in the long run. There is also the possibility that higher operating costs, such as rent for a second premises, might eventually be passed on to customers through increased prices.

On balance, I believe the bakery should proceed with its expansion, but with caution. It could preserve quality by training staff thoroughly at the original shop before opening the second one, and it could avoid undercutting competitors by positioning itself as a premium rather than a discount option. If these measures are taken, the expansion would benefit both the business and the wider community, making it a welcome development rather than a threat.

Some people believe the museum should focus on hands-on experiments and interactive workshops, while others think lectures by famous scientists and guided exhibitions would be more beneficial. _provenance.cefr_reasoning: This is a classic discursive 'discuss both views and give your opinion' essay task requiring at least 250 words in 40 minutes. body.model_answer:
Science museums play a vital role in inspiring young people, and their summer programmes can shape teenagers' attitudes towards science for years to come. While some argue that hands-on experiments are the most valuable component, others favour lectures and guided exhibitions. In my opinion, a successful programme should prioritise interactive activities, although lectures still have a supporting role to play.

There are strong reasons to favour hands-on experiments and workshops. First of all, teenagers learn best by doing rather than by listening. When students mix chemicals, build simple robots or dissect specimens themselves, abstract concepts become tangible and memorable. Secondly, interactive workshops develop practical skills such as teamwork, problem-solving and critical thinking, which are difficult to acquire in a lecture hall. Finally, the excitement of conducting a real experiment can spark a lifelong passion for science, something that passive observation rarely achieves.

On the other hand, supporters of lectures and exhibitions point out that renowned scientists can communicate cutting-edge research that no classroom experiment could cover. Listening to an inspiring speaker may motivate teenagers to pursue scientific careers, and guided tours expose them to achievements they could never recreate at a workbench. Moreover, lectures require fewer resources, allowing the museum to accommodate larger groups.

Nevertheless, I believe the drawbacks of a lecture-based programme outweigh its advantages. Teenagers on summer holiday are unlikely to remain engaged during long talks, whereas active participation guarantees attention and enjoyment. Ideally, the museum could combine both approaches, using short lectures to introduce topics and workshops to explore them in depth.

In conclusion, although lectures and exhibitions have their merits, a summer programme centred on hands-on experiments would benefit teenagers far more, provided that inspiring talks are used to complement, not replace, practical activities.

body.model_answer:
The question of whether mobile phones belong in classrooms has become increasingly controversial as these devices have become almost universal among students. While some educators argue for a total ban, others believe phones can enhance learning. In my view, a balanced approach that permits controlled use is the most sensible solution.

Supporters of a complete ban point to the obvious distractions phones create. Notifications from social media, games and messaging apps can easily pull students' attention away from lessons, and research suggests that multitasking with a phone significantly reduces concentration and academic performance. Furthermore, phones can facilitate cheating during tests and may encourage cyber-bullying during school hours. Teachers also find it difficult to monitor dozens of screens at once, which adds to their workload.

On the other hand, advocates of allowing phones argue that these devices are powerful educational tools. Students can instantly look up vocabulary, access online dictionaries, watch instructional videos or use interactive quizzes that make lessons more engaging. Phones also support inclusive learning, as students who cannot afford laptops can still access digital materials through their phones. In addition, keeping phones accessible allows parents to reach their children in emergencies, which reassures many families.

In my opinion, banning phones entirely ignores their genuine educational value, but unrestricted use is clearly harmful. Schools should therefore adopt clear policies: phones remain silent and out of sight during lectures, but teachers may invite students to use them for specific research tasks or interactive activities. This teaches students digital discipline, a skill they will certainly need at university and in the workplace.

In conclusion, rather than choosing between a total ban and free use, schools should regulate mobile phone use carefully. With sensible rules, phones can shift from being a classroom distraction to a valuable learning resource.

body.model_answer: In recent years, many cities have invested heavily in public parks, and the opening of a new park in my own city has sparked debate about whether such spending is justified. While hospitals and schools are undoubtedly essential, I believe that public parks are equally valuable and deserve continued investment. First of all, parks play a crucial role in public health. Green spaces encourage residents to exercise, whether by jogging, cycling or simply walking, which reduces the risk of obesity and heart disease. Moreover, spending time in nature has been proven to lower stress and improve mental well-being, which indirectly reduces the burden on the healthcare system. Secondly, parks strengthen communities. They provide a free meeting place where families, children and elderly residents can socialise, attend events and build relationships. In crowded urban areas where many people live in small apartments, such shared spaces are often the only place where neighbours can interact. This sense of community is something that money spent elsewhere rarely achieves. Admittedly, critics argue that basic services such as hospitals and schools should always come first, and this point has some merit. A city cannot function without educated citizens and adequate medical care. However, this is not an either-or choice: governments can and should budget for both. In fact, because parks are relatively cheap to build and maintain compared with hospitals, they offer excellent value for money. In conclusion, although hospitals and schools are vital, public parks deliver significant health, social and economic benefits at a modest cost. Rather than viewing the two as competing priorities, city authorities should treat green spaces as an essential part of urban infrastructure alongside other public services.
